Insularity

/in-suh-LAIR-ih-tee/ - the stress falls on LAIR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Insularity means narrow-mindedness caused by isolation from outside ideas.

The restaurant guide accused the city's chefs of insularity: no one had eaten anywhere but each other's dining rooms in years, and the menus showed it.

Worked Example

For decades the piano factory promoted only from the shop floor, subscribed to no trade journals, and sent no one to the fairs in Vienna. When customers began asking for the new quieter key actions, nobody inside had ever heard one. The firm's insularity had not felt like a decision; it had simply never occurred to anyone to look outward.

Insularity is not shyness, and it is more than being cut off: it is what being cut off does to thinking. The word points at the closed loop itself - the same ideas circulating among the same few people until nobody remembers there is an outside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

parochialism: Parochialism is the parish's narrowness — judging every question by local terms and local interests. Insularity is the condition that produces such narrowness anywhere: a group sealed off from outside ideas until its thinking closes. A parochial board weighs only local concerns; insularity explains why no other concerns arrive.

narrow-mindedness: Narrow-mindedness is closed thinking from any cause at all — stubbornness, vanity, fear, or plain habit. Insularity names one specific cause: isolation, the sealed loop that keeps outside ideas from ever arriving. Narrow-mindedness describes the closed mind itself; insularity blames the sealed environment around it.

provincialism: Provincialism is the narrowness of the provinces — tastes and judgments formed far from the capital, unaware of the wider world. Insularity needs no map: it can seal a famous kitchen, a firm, or a capital city itself, wherever a group stops looking outward.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

openness: willingness to let new ideas in

worldliness: experience of the wide world

Where it sits · how deeply a group seals itself off — wariness → cliquishness → insularity

wariness vs. insularity: Wariness toward outsiders is just caution, and it can be dropped in a moment; insularity has hardened into a way of thinking.

cliquishness vs. insularity: Cliquishness closes one small circle at lunch tables and group chats; insularity goes further, sealing a whole community's thinking against the outside.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — insul-

Root — insul-: island (Latin insula)

Suffix — -ar

Suffix — -ar: relating to

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state of being

Put it together

Put it together: Insul- (Latin insula, 'island') + -ar (relating to) + -ity (the state of being) = the state of being island-like. You met the adjective insular in the last unit; insularity is what the suffix -ity builds from it - island-mindedness as a condition. The island root also gives us insulate (to wrap something in its own protective island) and peninsula (an 'almost-island').

Use the root in a new word: peninsula

Use the root in a new word: peninsula: Florida is a peninsula - Latin for 'almost an island' - joined to the mainland along only one edge.

Word Choice

formal / academic

Insularity is the analyst's word - reviews, histories, and reports use it to explain why a group stopped taking in new ideas. Narrow-mindedness blames a person; insularity blames the sealed environment around them. You met the adjective insular in Unit 4: insular describes the group, insularity names the condition.
